parts:
HI All,

I have written a dynamic model predicting Democratic vote (attached). The problem: With a sample size of about 600,000 and 46 time-periods the model takes forever to run (about a week per 50 iterations). Is there any obvious ways to speed up the model?


Thanks,
Tobi

  int<lower=0> n_day;                                // number of party-categories

    for (i in 1:day_size[s]) {

Moving to non-centered parameterizations will probably help for
group-level parameters where you don't have many elements.

So instead of

gamma ~ foo(loc, scale);

use

gamma_raw ~ foo(0, 1);
gamma <- loc + scale * gamma_raw;

where gamma_raw is the parameter and gamma is a local variable.

Also, these:

> for (k in 2:n_day) {
> beta[k] ~ cauchy(beta[k-1], sigma_beta_evo);

are much more efficient as:

beta[2:n_day] ~ cauchy(beta[1:(n_day - 1)], sigma_beta_evo);

This:

> for (i in 1:day_size[s]) {
> real y_hat;
> y_hat <- alpha
> +beta[s]*female[obs_in_day[i]]
> +a_age[s,age[obs_in_day[i]]]
> +a_edu[s,edu[obs_in_day[i]]]
> +a_party_id[s,party_id[obs_in_day[i]]]
> +a_race[s,race[obs_in_day[i]]]+gamma*vote_prev_dma[i]
> +a_dma[s,dma[obs_in_day[i]]];
> y[obs_in_day[i]] ~ bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
> }

can be vectorized as:

y[obs_in_day] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha
+ beta[s] * female[obs_in_day]
+ ...);

If you make female a vector.

If female[...] is an indicator, then it's acutally more efficient to
build up that linear predictor using conditionals to avoid the unnecessary
multiplication by zero and useless derivative propagations.

- Bob

matrix[3,5] y;
matrix[3,5] mu;

That would be pushing Stan to the limit even if the model were
more cleanly identified. As is, this linear predictor

> y[obs_in_day] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha
> +beta[s]*female[obs_in_day]
> +to_vector(a_age[s,age[obs_in_day]])
> +to_vector(a_edu[s,edu[obs_in_day]])
> +to_vector(a_party_id[s,party_id[obs_in_day]])
> +to_vector(a_race[s,race[obs_in_day]])
> +gamma*vote_prev_dma[obs_in_day]
> +to_vector(a_dma[s,dma[obs_in_day]]));
> }}

is only weakly identified because of all the varying
intercepts.

Have you thought about only including intercepts for some
of the alternatives? That is, if there are 5 age cohorts,
only include predictors for four of them and roll the last
into the intercept --- it can help with identification. But
even with this kind of recoding, this scale of data's probably
more than Stan can handle.

Otherwise, I don't see any alternative other than subsampling
the data to fit, fitting pieces of the model separately, or
moving to an approximate algorithm like ADVI (which we don't
understand well in terms of how fits relate to the full Bayesian
posterior).

- Bob

On Wednesday, May 4, 2016 at 7:27:02 PM UTC-7, Bob Carpenter wrote:
That would be pushing Stan to the limit even if the model were
more cleanly identified.  As is, this linear predictor


>  y[obs_in_day] ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha

>       +gamma*vote_prev_dma[obs_in_day]
>       +to_vector(a_dma[s,dma[obs_in_day]]));
>   }}

is only weakly identified because of all the varying
intercepts.

Have you thought about only including intercepts for some
of the alternatives?  That is, if there are 5 age cohorts,
only include predictors for four of them and roll the last
into the intercept --- it can help with identification.  But
even with this kind of recoding, this scale of data's probably
more than Stan can handle.

Otherwise, I don't see any alternative other than subsampling
the data to fit, fitting pieces of the model separately, or
moving to an approximate algorithm like ADVI (which we don't
understand well in terms of how fits relate to the full Bayesian
posterior).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Speeding up Dynamic Regression Model with many time-periods and big sample size
parts:
1) For the dynamic part of the model, why not try a normal distribution instead of a Cauchy/t distribution?  If this gives you much faster results, it tells you something about the evolution process.

2) Is there any way you can aggregate the individuals into groups (eg # of people in a certain age bin, # of people in a certain party ID etc) and then use a binomial likelihood instead of a bernoulli likelihood?  This way you will have a much smaller number of data points to loop over.   This effectively means you are doing binomial regression.  Assuming you have 10 age bins, 5 edu bins, 3 race bins, 2 party ID bins, 2 DMA bins (I don't know what DMA is), and 2 gender bins, this is a maximum of 1200 unique bins.  This means that your likelihood has 500x less terms in the calculation, so you should expect a substantial speedup.  Explanation for this mathematically is here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_regression#In_terms_of_binomial_data

3) To go further down this path, if you do binomial regression and your sample size in each bin is large enough, you can approximate the binomial likelihood with a Gaussian, and then apply the Kalman filter to solve your problem in one go (as a Dynamic Linear Model).  Note that Stan now appears to have a function for this directly - gaussian_dlm_obs, so the effort in coding the DLM should be fairly low. 

4) As noted by others you are going to run into identifiability problems here because of multicollinearity in the predictors.  I ran into this problem recently - see here.  You need to drop one out of each of the predictors so that your predictors are linearly independent.  Although the Bayesian priors in theory solve the identifiability issue, you'll find that your posteriors have extremely high correlations on these parameters (probably >0.99), so that the standard NUTS sampling will be very slow.  A dense mass matrix will solve this, but you'll never be able to get enough posterior samples to estimate the mass matrix reliability (ie chicken and egg problem), so in practice dropping one out of each of the predictors and folding it into the intercept as suggested is a much better option. 



The advantage of using the Kalman filter for the evolving parameters is that it integrates out the random walk of the parameters directly, giving an analytical formula for the posterior.

parts: Also, note that by doing this problem as suggested via binomial regression, rather than logistic regression, the number of terms in the likelihood becomes independent of sample size.

On Sunday, 8 May 2016 15:06:10 UTC+10, Julian King wrote:
1) For the dynamic part of the model, why not try a normal distribution instead of a Cauchy/t distribution?  If this gives you much faster results, it tells you something about the evolution process.

2) Is there any way you can aggregate the individuals into groups (eg # of people in a certain age bin, # of people in a certain party ID etc) and then use a binomial likelihood instead of a bernoulli likelihood?  This way you will have a much smaller number of data points to loop over.   This effectively means you are doing binomial regression.  Assuming you have 10 age bins, 5 edu bins, 3 race bins, 2 party ID bins, 2 DMA bins (I don't know what DMA is), and 2 gender bins, this is a maximum of 1200 unique bins.  This means that your likelihood has 500x less terms in the calculation, so you should expect a substantial speedup.  Explanation for this mathematically is here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_regression#In_terms_of_binomial_data

3) To go further down this path, if you do binomial regression and your sample size in each bin is large enough, you can approximate the binomial likelihood with a Gaussian, and then apply the Kalman filter to solve your problem in one go (as a Dynamic Linear Model).  Note that Stan now appears to have a function for this directly - gaussian_dlm_obs, so the effort in coding the DLM should be fairly low. 

4) As noted by others you are going to run into identifiability problems here because of multicollinearity in the predictors.  I ran into this problem recently - see here.  You need to drop one out of each of the predictors so that your predictors are linearly independent.  Although the Bayesian priors in theory solve the identifiability issue, you'll find that your posteriors have extremely high correlations on these parameters (probably >0.99), so that the standard NUTS sampling will be very slow.  A dense mass matrix will solve this, but you'll never be able to get enough posterior samples to estimate the mass matrix reliability (ie chicken and egg problem), so in practice dropping one out of each of the predictors and folding it into the intercept as suggested is a much better option. 



The advantage of using the Kalman filter for the evolving parameters is that it integrates out the random walk of the parameters directly, giving an analytical formula for the posterior.

Hi, I have 3 thoughts. First, yes, subset the data for sure.  We have ideas of how to do this more formally (see here: http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/ep.pdf), but even a simple partitioning will often make sense.  Second, strip down your model.  Remove most of these varying intercepts. Start with a model with only one of these sigmas.  That should run fast.  Then add them, one at a time, and see how that goes.
Third, once you start to add in these factors, start by giving them fixed values of sigma.  For example, sigma=0.1 or 0.2.  Remember, excluding a factor is just sigma=0.  In lots of these examples, these sigmas aren't so well identified anyway.  Run the models with fixed sigmas, that should be fast.  In fact, with fixed sigmas this is just a logistic regression model with a prior, you could even do point estimation, perhaps.  Then replaces some of the fixed sigmas with priors, etc.  Build up to it.  Ideally the entire process should just take a few days.

10 iterations a day is ridiculous:  there's no way you should trust your model enough to sit around and wait like that.  I'd have more confidence in a model with externally-supplied sigmas that could run fast so you could try out different possibilities.

Also this example could be a good candidate for GMO, perhaps.
